questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman presented with a rash on her finger. It had been present for 2 months and had not improved. There was no history of fevers, and the rash was not painful or draining. She had a past medical history of type 2 diabetes. She lived in Chicago and had not travelled in recent years. She was a carpenter and recalled pulling a wooden splinter out of that finger about 1 month before the rash developed. She lived with her partner and 8-year-old son, who were both well. They had a pet dog and cat that were healthy and owned several exotic fish; the patient sometimes helped her son clean the tank. On examination, there was an erythematous lesion that was not tender, warm, or fluctuant. There were no other skin lesions present. Investigations: Plain radiograph of the hand showed no fracture or foreign body.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Itraconazole The most likely diagnosis in this case is sporotrichosis, notably the fixed cutaneous form as there is no mention of the typical lymphangitic pattern of nodules along the ipsilateral limb. Although she does occasionally clean her son’s fish tank (consider Mycobacterium marinum ) and owns a cat (consider Bartonella henselae or cat scratch disease) the most important clue is the history of the wooden splinter that she removed from her finger one month prior to this, suggesting direct inoculation with Sporothrix. It is also possible, and often more common, for cats to transmit Sporothrix with a scratch (particularly cats that spend time outdoors with soil contamination of their claws); although still plausible, there is no mention of a cat scratch. The prolonged duration of symptoms and findings argue against this being a pyogenic (e.g., staphylococcal) infection. Sporotrichosis does not resolve without treatment. A skin biopsy for histopathology and fungal culture should confirm the diagnosis. Treatment with itraconazole is recommended for a total duration of 3–6 months until all lesions have fully resolved for at least 2–4 weeks. (Image from Cohen BA. Nodules and tumors. In Pediatric Dermatology. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2013.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q30

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Mycobacterium marinum (2) Sporothrix schenckii (3) Nocardia brasiliensis (4) Leishmania braziliensis (also Francisella tularensis). b) Mycobacterium marinum (fish-tank/aquarium exposure). c) Skin biopsy of a lesion for histopathology plus mycobacterial culture at 30-32 C (with AFB stain); culture is the diagnostic standard.
questions.beyond_mandell: M. marinum and nodular-lymphangitis differential are outside this Sporothrix slice; based on standard mycobacterial/IDSA teaching.

cohort_answer.text: Differential: Mycobacterium marinum; Sporothrix schenckii; Nocardia brasiliensis; Leishmania braziliensis; Tularemia; Systemic mycoses. Most likely: Mycobacterium marinum. Diagnosis: Biopsy for AFB and culture + histopath. Treatment: surgical debridement/excision should suffice, if invasive, give rifampin + ethambutol +/- macrolide

What treatment would you start if the Gram stain showed yeast?

What treatment would you start if the gram stain showed yeast?

questions.model_answer: a) Long Gram-positive bacilli in a lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) ulcer indicate Nocardia (most often Nocardia brasiliensis). Localized cutaneous disease in the immunocompetent host is treated with oral TMP-SMX as the preferred monotherapy (alternatives per susceptibility: minocycline, amoxicillin-clavulanate, a fluoroquinolone, or a macrolide). b) Yeast in a sporotrichoid ulcer indicates Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichosis); start oral itraconazole.
questions.beyond_mandell: The yeast/Sporothrix arm and itraconazole are not covered in this Nocardia chapter (standard sporotrichosis management, IDSA sporotrichosis guideline).

cohort_answer.text: Long GPB: TMP-SMX/imipenem/amikacin for ?nocardia; ?anthrax for cipro/doxy. || Yeast: Sporothrix schenkii, itraconazole.

cohort_answer.text: Mycobacterium marinum. Monotherapy options: Clarithromycin, or Doxycycline/Minocycline, or Septra for minimum 3 months; rifampin plus ethambutol. Other lymphocutaneous organisms: Francisella tularensis, Nocardia brasiliensis, Mycobacterium marinum, other NTM, Sporothrix schenckii, Leishmaniasis, Bacillus anthracis. (Note: Sandford combination therapy is 2 active agents for 1-2 months after resolution of skin lesion: Clarithromycin 500mg BID + ethambutol 25mg/kg/day, or Rifampin 600mg q24h + ethambutol 25mg/kg/day; Hopkins offers monotherapy alternatives: minocycline 100 BID, doxycycline 100 BID, Septra DS BID.)

questions.question: A renal transplant recipient with diabetes cut his hand at a lake house. One week later he developed papules and ulcerative lesions on the hand and arm without lymphatic involvement. Pathology shows granulomatous inflammation with a soccer-ball appearance (morulae); AFB and bacterial stains are negative. Sabouraud agar grows a white fluffy colony at 6 days.

Pathology shows granulomatous inflammation with soccer ball appearance (morulae). AFB and bacterial negative. Sabouraud agar shows white fluffy colony at 6 days.

parts.text: What is the most likely genus?
What group of organisms does this belong to?
What are two treatments?

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely genus?

questions.model_answer: a) Prototheca (the morula/soccer-ball sporangia with internal endospores and water/lake exposure are characteristic; the absence of lymphatic spread argues against classic sporotrichoid disease). b) Achlorophyllous (colourless) green algae. c) (1) Amphotericin B (lipid formulation); (2) an azole - itraconazole or fluconazole (surgical excision of localized lesions is adjunctive).
questions.beyond_mandell: Protothecosis is not covered in this Sporothrix slice; morphology and therapy per standard Mandell/CMR protothecosis teaching.

questions.model_answer: a) Leishmania spp. amastigotes (intracellular, 1-5 microns, with nucleus and kinetoplast, within macrophages). b) Nocardia spp. (branching, filamentous, beaded gram-positive rods). c) Francisella tularensis (tiny gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey; oxidase-negative). d) Sporothrix schenckii (small ~1-3 micron cigar-shaped budding yeast; ovoid conidia on conidiophores in mould phase).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Sporothrix cigar-shaped yeast morphology is grounded in the slice (p. 3134); the other identifications are standard microbiology.

cohort_answer.text:
Image 1: Leishmania spp. amastigotes, H&E stain - spherical to ovoid, 1-5 µm long by 1-2 µm wide, large nucleus, prominent kinetoplast, short axoneme (rarely visible by light microscopy); reside in macrophages.
Image 2: Nocardia - branching, filamentous, beaded, gram-positive rods with right angle branching (compare/contrast with Rhodococcus equi).
Image 3: Francisella tularensis - tiny, gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey; 'junky' gram stain of tiny GNCB's, DDx Francisella or Brucella; oxidase negative, urease negative, weakly catalase positive, strict aerobes.
Image 4: Sporothrix schenckii - small (~2 microns); PAS stained tissue section showing budding yeast-like cells; conidiophores and conidia are ovoid, elongated, 3-6 x 2-3 µm, one-celled, smooth walled, hyaline.
